This is game 2 in a series of 9×9 Go games. Each new game starts in a fresh session.

## Your goal

To become as strong at Go as you can: to keep improving, game after game, toward grandmaster-level play. The concrete target is to win consistently against the strongest opponent on the ladder, the 9d profile.

## What carries over

This session starts with no memory of the earlier ones: your conversation is not carried over. Your working directory does carry over: every file in it stays as you leave it. If CLAUDE.md exists there, it is loaded into your context at the start of every session; your other files are there to read with the file tools. What a later session knows of your earlier games is what you have left in these files.

Your working directory holds:
- CLAUDE.md (2,019 bytes)
- games.md (711 bytes)

## This game

A new game. You play White, so your opponent moves first, right after you choose it.

Rules: Chinese area scoring, with 7 points of komi for White; a level score is a draw. Simple ko: an immediate recapture is refused, and the board marks the ko point when there is one. Suicide is not allowed. An invalid move is refused with the rule it broke, and the turn stays with you. The game ends after two passes in a row or a resignation; a game that reaches 243 moves is scored where it stands. After two passes the engine scores the position as it stands and decides itself which stones are dead.

## Opponents

Your opponent is KataGo playing in the style of a human of the rank you choose. The ladder, weakest to strongest: 20k, 18k, 16k, 14k, 12k, 10k, 8k, 6k, 4k, 2k, 1d, 3d, 5d, 7d, 9d. You choose the rank with `choose_opponent(rank)` before the first move; it holds for the whole game, and you choose again in the next game.

## Tools

- Go: `choose_opponent(rank)`, `board()`, `play(move)` with a point or `pass`, and `resign()`.
- Files: your Read, Write, Edit, Glob and Grep tools, for any file in your working directory.

You also have a shell, and you may write and run code in it; Python is available as `python3`. Use it only to inspect the current position and keep records — for example, to count stones or liberties, or check whether a move is legal. Do not build or use a Go engine, run Monte Carlo, search over sequences of future moves, or write a program that chooses, ranks or recommends moves.

## How this session ends

Play until the game is over. The final result comes back from your last Go call, followed by a closing note. Before you end the session after a game, write down in your working directory whatever will help the next session play better. The session ends when you end your turn.

# Go notes (9x9 vs KataGo human-style) — READ FIRST

See `games.md` for the per-game log. Update both files after every game.
Color alternates per game (G1 Black, G2 White). Check the prompt for which color you are.

## Ladder status
- Game 1: Black vs 8k, lost W+14 (Black 37 area).
- Game 2: White vs 8k, lost B+12 (White ~31 area + 7 komi vs 50).
- Next suggestion: drop to 10k or 12k to get a first win and learn what works, then climb.

## Key facts
- Komi 7, area scoring. Black needs >= 44 of 81. White needs >= 38 area (37 = draw).
- Area scoring: playing inside the opponent's territory late costs nothing, so probing
  invasions at the end are free (but they rarely work vs correct answers).
- Opponent passes when the game is settled; engine removes dead stones itself.

## THE BIG RECURRING PROBLEM (both games)
I build a long center wall and the opponent takes two corners/sides. A center wall does NOT
score on 9x9. In both games I ended with ~31-37 points of mostly stones.
=> Fix: prioritize CORNERS and SIDES. Each time, ask "which corner/side is still open?"
   and take it before pressing/attaching in the center. Count at move ~15: if my likely
   territory is < 38 (White) / < 44 (Black), I must take a side, not strengthen the center.
- Game 2: B G7 (upper right), I played E5 tengen, B attached F5, I made F4/G4/E4 shape;
  Black then took lower-left with C4/C5/D3 in sente. Try instead: answer G7 with a corner
  move (C3 / C4 / D3 area), or after the F5 attachment, take the empty lower-left corner first.

## Lessons
1. CHECK LIBERTIES OF MY OWN STONES before every move, especially after the opponent plays
   adjacent — AND count libs of the stone I am about to place (with its group). Game 2: W J6
   made a 2-stone group with 1 liberty; Black captured immediately. Game 1: lost G4 in atari.
2. Don't throw in cutting stones that end with 1-2 libs inside the opponent's area (G1 B7/B4,
   G2 H7). Read the capturing race first: count my libs vs theirs, who moves next.
3. When behind on count by 10+, identify the weakest enemy group EARLY (before it settles).
   Black's lower-left in G2 was loose (C4,C5,D3,C2,E2,F2 all separate) around move 20-25;
   that was the moment to attack, not at the end.
4. A 1-wide strip of 4 on the edge (straight four) is alive; don't waste moves there.
5. Good things that worked: capturing-race reading on G3/H3 (W F3 atari, H2, H4, J3 capture).

## Process checklist each move
- What did the opponent's last move threaten? (Count libs of all my groups next to it.)
- Any of my groups at 1-2 libs? Any of theirs? Libs of the stone I'm about to play?
- Rough count (write a quick ownership map in python): who is ahead? If behind, play
  bigger: open corners/sides first, then attack weak groups.
